facts.statement: The Rodrigues starling was first reported by French sailor Julien Tafforet, who was marooned on Rodrigues between 1725 and 1726.
facts.quote: The bird was only reported by French sailor Julien Tafforet, who was marooned on the island from 1725 to 1726.

facts.statement: Subfossil remains of the Rodrigues starling found on the mainland were scientifically described in 1879.
facts.quote: Subfossil remains found on the mainland were described in 1879, and were suggested to belong to the bird mentioned by Tafforet.

facts.statement: The Rodrigues starling measured 25 to 30 cm in length and possessed a stout beak.
facts.quote: The Rodrigues starling was 25–30 cm long, and had a stout beak.

facts.statement: The Rodrigues starling ate eggs and dead tortoises, which it processed using its strong bill.
facts.quote: Its diet included eggs and dead tortoises, which it processed with its strong bill.

facts.statement: It is believed that predation by introduced rats caused the extinction of the Rodrigues starling in the 18th century.
facts.quote: Predation by rats introduced to the area was probably responsible for the bird's extinction some time in the 18th century.

facts.statement: The Rodrigues starling was an extinct species endemic to the Mascarene island of Rodrigues.
facts.quote: The Rodrigues starling (Necropsar rodericanus) is an extinct species of starling that was endemic to the Mascarene island of Rodrigues.

facts.statement: Subfossil bones of the bird were first discovered by George Jenner in 1866 and 1871, and by Henry H. Slater in 1874.
facts.quote: Subfossil bones of a starling-like bird were first discovered on Rodrigues by the police magistrate George Jenner In 1866 and 1871, and by the British naturalist Henry H. Slater in 1874.

facts.statement: The subfossil bones were found in caves on the Plaine Coral, a limestone plain in south-west Rodrigues.
facts.quote: They were found in caves on the Plaine Coral, a limestone plain in south-west Rodrigues.

facts.statement: The species was named Necropsar rodericanus, derived from Greek words for "dead" and "starling" and the name of the island Rodrigues.
facts.quote: They named the bird Necropsar rodericanus; Nekros and psar are Greek for "dead" and "starling", while rodericanus refers to the island of Rodrigues.

facts.statement: It was debated by Masauji Hachisuka whether the subfossils described by Günther and Newton belonged to the bird reported by Tafforet, based on differences in diet and crest presence.
facts.quote: Hachisuka believed the carnivorous habits described by Tafforet to be unlikely for a starling, and thought the lack of a crest suggested that it was not closely related to Fregilupus, and therefore concluded that the bones described by Günther and Newton did not belong to the bird mentioned by Tafforet.

facts.statement: The Rodrigues starling went extinct on the mainland first, with Île Gombrani serving as its final refuge.
facts.quote: It first became extinct on mainland Rodrigues, then on Île Gombrani, its last refuge.

facts.statement: The bird was observed by Tafforet on the offshore islet of Île Gombrani.
facts.quote: Tafforet observed it on the offshore islet of Île Gombrani.

facts.statement: Günther and Newton considered the species likely identical to the bird described by Tafforet due to its strongly built bill.
facts.quote: Due to the strongly built bill, they considered the new species likely the same as the bird mentioned in Tafforet's account.

facts.statement: Subfossils found in 1974 supported the classification of the Rodrigues starling as a distinct genus.
facts.quote: More subfossils found in 1974 added support to the claim that the Rodrigues bird was a distinct genus of starling.

facts.statement: Julian P. Hume designated the skull specimen NMHUK A9050 as the lectotype because Günther and Newton had not originally designated a holotype.
facts.quote: Hume noted that Günther and Newton had not designated a holotype specimen among the fossils they based the specific name on, and chose the skull from their syntype series of bones as the lectotype; specimen NMHUK A9050, housed at the Natural History Museum, London.

facts.statement: The Rodrigues starling measured between 25 and 30 centimeters in length, which was large for a starling.
facts.quote: The Rodrigues starling was large for a starling, being 25–30 cm in length.

facts.statement: The skull was similar in size to that of the hoopoe starling, but the overall skeleton was smaller.
facts.quote: The skull of the Rodrigues starling was similar to and about the same size as that of the hoopoe starling, but the skeleton was smaller.

facts.statement: Its maxilla was shorter and less curved than the hoopoe starling's, with a stouter mandible.
facts.quote: The maxilla of the Rodrigues starling was shorter, less curved, had a less slender tip, and had a stouter mandible.

facts.statement: The bill measured 36 to 39 millimeters in length and was less curved and deeper than that of the hoopoe starling.
facts.quote: The bill was about 36–39 mm long, less curved and proportionally a little deeper than in the hoopoe starling.

facts.statement: The lower jaw was approximately 52 to 60 millimeters long and 4 to 5 millimeters deep at the rear.
facts.quote: The mandible was about 52–60 mm long and 4–5 mm deep at the back.

facts.statement: The development of the supraoccipital ridge indicates the bird possessed strong neck and jaw muscles.
facts.quote: This indicates that the starling had strong neck and jaw muscles.

facts.statement: The upper arm bone was slender, curved, and measured 32 to 35 millimeters long.
facts.quote: The humerus was gracile and had a curved shaft, and measured 32–35 mm.

facts.statement: The thigh bone was large and robust, measuring approximately 33 millimeters in length.
facts.quote: The femur measured around 33 mm.

facts.statement: The ankle bone was long and robust with a straight shaft, measuring 36 to 41 millimeters.
facts.quote: The tarsometatarsus (ankle bone) was long, robust, with a relatively straight shaft, and measured 36–41 mm.

facts.statement: Although capable of flight, the bird had a smaller sternum than other starlings, suggesting it did not require powerful flight due to the island's small size and topography.
facts.quote: Though the Rodrigues starling was clearly able to fly, its sternum was smaller compared to that of other starlings; it may not have required powerful flight, due to the small area and topography of Rodrigues.

facts.statement: Robust limbs and strong jaws indicate the bird foraged on the ground.
facts.quote: The robustness of its limbs and the strong jaws with the ability to gape indicates that it foraged on the ground.

facts.statement: The bird likely used its wedge-shaped bill to open entrances and remove objects while searching for food, similar to other starlings and crows.
facts.quote: It probably also had the ability to remove objects and forcefully open entrances when searching for food; it did this by inserting its wedge-shaped bill and opening its mandibles, as other starlings and crows do.

facts.statement: Its feeding adaptations support historical observations that the bird ate eggs and dead tortoises.
facts.quote: This ability supports Tafforet's observation that the bird fed on eggs and dead tortoises.

facts.statement: Historical descriptions indicate the bird possessed a complex song.
facts.quote: Tafforet's description also indicates that it had a complex song.

facts.statement: The species was extinct by the time of the 1761 French Transit of Venus expedition.
facts.quote: The Rodrigues starling was extinct by the time French scientist Alexandre Guy Pingré visited Rodrigues during the French 1761 Transit of Venus expedition.

facts.statement: The bird was described by Tafforet, who was familiar with the fauna of Réunion.
facts.quote: Tafforet was familiar with the fauna of Réunion, where the related hoopoe starling lived.

facts.statement: The species belongs to the genus Necropsar.
facts.quote: genus: Necropsar

facts.statement: The scientific name of the species is Necropsar rodericanus.
facts.quote: species: N. rodericanus

facts.statement: The binomial authority is attributed to Günther and E. Newton in 1879.
facts.quote: binomial_authority: Günther y Newton, 1879 vide Slater

facts.statement: It is debated whether the bird was sexually dimorphic due to insufficient fossil remains.
facts.quote: Not enough remains of the Rodrigues starling have been found to assess whether it was sexually dimorphic.

facts.statement: The Rodrigues starling (Necropsar rodericanus) was an extinct passerine bird of the Sturnidae family endemic to Rodrigues Island in the Mascarene archipelago of the southwest Indian Ocean.
facts.quote: El estornino de Rodrigues (Necropsar rodericanus) es una especie extinta de ave paseriforme de la familia Sturnidae endémica de la isla de Rodrigues, del archipiélago de las Mascareñas en el suroeste del Índico.

facts.statement: The bird measured 25–30 cm in length and possessed a long, robust beak.
facts.quote: El estornino de Rodrigues medía entre 25–30 cm de largo, y tenía un pico largo y robusto.

facts.statement: Its only record describes plumage with a white body, black wings and tail, and yellow beak and legs.
facts.quote: En su único registro se afirma que tenía el plumaje del cuerpo de color blanco, con las alas y cola en parte negras, y el pico y las patas amarillos.

facts.statement: Its diet included eggs and dead turtles, which it tore apart with its strong beak.
facts.quote: Su dieta incluía huevos y tortugas muertas, que despedazaba con su fuerte pico.

facts.statement: The bird was sighted only once, by French sailor Julien Tafforet, who was stranded on the island between 1725 and 1726.
facts.quote: El avistamiento del estornino de Rodrigues sólo fue registrado una vez, por el marinero francés Julien Tafforet, que fue abandonado en la isla entre 1725 y 1726.

facts.statement: Subfossil bones were discovered in 1866 and 1871 by magistrate George Jenner and in 1874 by Reverend Henry Horrocks Slater.
facts.quote: Se descubrieron huesos subfósiles de un pájaro similar a un estornino de Reunión en 1866 y 1871, por el magistrado policial George Jenner, y en 1874, por el reverendo Henry Horrocks Slater.

facts.statement: The fossils were found in caves in the Plaine Coral limestone plain in southwest Rodrigues.
facts.quote: Se encontraron en cuevas de Plaine Coral, una planicie caliza en el suroeste de Rodrigues.

facts.statement: In 1879, ornithologists Albert Günther and Edward Newton used these bones to scientifically describe the bird.
facts.quote: En 1879 estos huesos fueron la base para la descripción científica del ave de los ornitólogos Albert Günther y Edward Newton (el hermano de Alfred).

facts.statement: They named it Necropsar rodericanus, derived from Greek terms for 'dead' and 'starling' and the Latin adjective for Rodrigues Island.
facts.quote: Lo nombraron Necropsar rodericanus. Nekros y psar son los términos griegos para «muerto» y «estornino», respectivamente, mientras que rodericanus es el gentilicio latino para la isla de Rodrigues.

facts.statement: Tafforet observed that the bird lived on the islet of Gombrani located south of Rodrigues.
facts.quote: Tafforet observó que vivía en el islote Gombrani ubicado al sur de Rodrigues.

facts.statement: In 1967, ornithologist James Greenway suggested the bird should belong to the same genus as the Réunion starling, Fregilupus, due to similarities between the two species.
facts.quote: En 1967 el ornitólogo estadounidense James Greenway sugirió que el estornino de Rodrigues debería pertenecer al mismo género del estornino de Reunión, Fregilupus, debido a las similitudes entre las dos especies.

facts.statement: In 1974, additional subfossils increased support for the hypothesis that the Rodrigues starling was a distinct genus.
facts.quote: En 1974 se encontraron más subfósiles que incrementaron el apoyo a la hipótesis de que el estornino de Rodrigues era un género distinto.

facts.statement: In 2014, paleontologist Julian P. Hume described a new extinct species, the Mauritius starling (Cryptopsar ischyrhynchus), based on subfossils from Mauritius.
facts.quote: En 2014 el paleontólogo británico Julian P. Hume describió una nueva especie extinta, el estornino de Mauricio (Cryptopsar ischyrhynchus), basándose en subfósiles de la isla de Mauricio.

facts.statement: This new species appeared closer to the Rodrigues starling than to the Réunion starling based on skull, sternum, and humerus characteristics.
facts.quote: Esta nueva especie parecía más cercana al estornino de Rodrigues que al estornino de Reunión, por las características de su cráneo, esternón y húmero.

facts.statement: In 1898, naturalist Henry Ogg Forbes described a second species, N. leguati, based on a dried skin specimen from the World Museum of Liverpool labeled as coming from Madagascar.
facts.quote: En 1898 el naturalista británico Henry Ogg Forbes describió una segunda especie atribuida al género Necropsar, N. leguati, basándose en una piel disecada del World Museum de Liverpool, espécimen D.1792, que estaba etiquetado como procedente de Madagascar.

facts.statement: In 2005, an DNA study identified the specimen as an albino gray cuckooshrike (Cinclocerthia gutturalis) from Martinica.
facts.quote: En 2005 un estudio de ADN lo identificó como un ejemplar albino de cocobino gris (Cinclocerthia gutturalis) de Martinica.

facts.statement: Hachisuka believed the carnivorous habits described by Tafforet were unlikely for a starling and that the lack of a crest indicated it was not closely related to Fregilupus.
facts.quote: Hachisuka creía que los hábitos carnívoros descritos por Tafforet eran poco probables para un estornino, y que la ausencia de penacho del pájaro de la descripción indicaba que no estaba cercanamente emparentado con Fregilupus.

facts.statement: Hachisuka's assumptions are now discredited, and modern ornithologists consider Tafforet's bird to be the same as the one described from subfossil remains.
facts.quote: Las suposiciones de Hachisuka actualmente están desacreditadas, y los ornitólogos modernos consideran que el pájaro de Tafforet es el mismo que el descrito a partir de los restos subfósiles.

facts.statement: In 1987, ornithologist Graham S. Cowles drafted a manuscript describing a new species of timaliidae, Rodriguites microcarina, based on a sternum found in a Rodrigues cave.
facts.quote: En 1987 el ornitólogo británico Graham S. Cowles elaboró un manuscrito que describía una nueva especie de timalíido, Rodriguites microcarina, basada en un esternón encontrado en una cueva de Rodrigues.

facts.statement: A subsequent examination of the Rodriguites microcarina sternum by Hume showed it actually belonged to a Rodrigues starling.
facts.quote: El examen posterior del esternón de Rodriguites microcarina realizado por Hume demostró que en realidad pertenecía a un estornino de Rodrigues.

facts.statement: Its body was white or whitish-grey, with dark brown wings and yellow legs and beak.
facts.quote: Su cuerpo era blanco o gris blanquecino, con las alas de color pardo negruzco, y las patas y el pico amarillos.

facts.statement: The mandible measured between 52–60 mm in length and about 4–5 mm in proximal depth.
facts.quote: La mandíbula medía entre 52–60 mm de largo y unos 4–5 mm de profundidad proximal.

facts.statement: Its humerus measured 32–35 mm, and the keel of its sternum was a bit lower.
facts.quote: Su húmero medía 32–35 mm, y la quilla de su esternón era un poco más baja.

facts.statement: A coracoid measuring 27.5 mm in length and a carpometacarpus measuring 22.5 mm have been measured.
facts.quote: Se ha medido un coracoides, siendo de 27,5 mm de largo, y un carpometacarpo que medía 22,5 mm.

facts.statement: The femur measured around 33 mm, the tibiotarsus 52–59 mm, and the tarsometatarsus 36–41 mm.
facts.quote: El fémur medía alrededor de 33 mm, el tibiotarso 52–59 mm, y el tarsometatarso 36–41 mm.

facts.statement: The robustness of its legs and beak indicates that it foraged for food on the ground.
facts.quote: La robustez de sus patas y su pico indica que buscaba alimento en el suelo.

facts.statement: Its diet could have consisted of various snails and other invertebrates of Rodrigues, as well as carrion.
facts.quote: Su dieta podría componerse de los diversos caracoles y demás invertebrados de Rodrigues, además de las carroñas.

facts.statement: Tafforet reported that pigeons and parrots from the southern coastal islets only went to the main island to drink water, and Leguat noted that pigeons only bred on the islets due to persecution by rats on the main island, suggesting the starlings might have done the same.
facts.quote: Tafforet informó que las palomas y los loros de los islotes frente a la costa sur solo iban a la isla principal para beber agua, y Leguat anotó que las palomas solo criaban en los islotes debido a la persecución que sufrían por parte de las ratas de la isla principal, por lo que los estorninos podrían haber hecho lo mismo.

facts.statement: Tafforet's description also indicates that it had a complex song.
facts.quote: La descripción de Tafforet también indica que tenía un canto complejo.

facts.statement: This ability supports Tafforet's assertion that they fed on eggs and dead turtles.
facts.quote: Esta capacidad apoya la afirmación de Tafforet de que se alimentaban de huevos y tortugas muertas.
